content: Labor experts stunned at how anti-worker Trump has been with actions since last Labor Day that have hurt unions Donald Trump has repeatedly vowed to champion US workers. Shortly before Labor Day last year, he said: “Every policy of the Trump administration is designed to lift up the American worker and “promote great-paying blue-collar jobs”. But in the year since last Labor Day, Trump has taken many actions that have hurt US workers and unions, with some labor experts saying they’ve been stunned at how anti-worker Trump has been. In the months after Trump returned to office, the Occupational Safety and Health Administration ( Osha) cut workplace inspections by 20% , compared with Joe Biden’s last year in office. Even though Trump campaigned as a champion of coal miners, his administration has repeatedly delayed implementation of a rule to limit silica dust , which has afflicted and killed many coal miners with black lung. The United Mine Workers union has urgently called for “immediate enforcement” of the stalled silica dust rule. Continue reading...
title: ‘The most anti-union president’: how Trump turned his back on US workers
author: Steven Greenhouse

content: It turns out most of us no longer believe in progress. And when that happens, it quickly becomes a crisis for societies like ours Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Depending on your politics, the monsters are everywhere. Perhaps you see them in the form of tech billionaires and the artificial intelligence they’re developing. Perhaps you see them in the bin fire of social media they bequeathed us before that, or the legacy media that refuse to tell you “the truth”. You might see them in the manosphere, or the institutions teaching our kids gender fluidity. Maybe you see them in the migrant youth wielding machetes in the suburbs, or the refugee attempting to behead someone on a Belfast street. Or perhaps you see them in the violent anti-immigrant mobs that torched houses in response. If so, you’ll likely see them in the March for Australia or the Unite the Kingdom rallies, organised by far-right groups but attended by many more besides. You’ll almost certainly see them in at least one of Hamas, Israel or those local advocates at each other’s throats over the Middle East. I suspect you’ll see them in Russia but that can no longer be assumed. And I’d guess that you’d see them in at least one political party with a significant share of the vote. Something in that paragraph probably outraged you. In which case, you’re probably seeing monsters in whoever sees different monsters from you. It would be easy here to make a point about polarisation. But I want to look at the deep disquiet that lies underneath. Continue reading...
title: That sound you hear is not the world ending – it’s liberalism being monstered | Waleed Aly
author: Waleed Aly

content: Russia attacked Kyiv with ballistic missiles on Tuesday, after U.S. envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner visited Ukraine's capital as part of an effort to resume stalled peace negotiations. Ukrainian officials said the attack involved ballistic and cruise missiles, according to CNN, and residential buildings in two districts of the city sustained damage as people were urged to remain indoors. Kyiv’s mayor, Vitali Klitschko, said people were trapped inside a residential building after the attacks. RUSSIA LAUNCHES BALLISTIC MISSILE ATTACK ON KYIV HOURS AFTER ZELENSKYY WARNS OF MAJOR STRIKE The attacks, which caused fires across the city, including at an educational facility, came after Witkoff and Kushner met with Ukrainian officials in Kyiv on Sunday. The day prior, they met with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow as the Trump administration attempts to bring an end to the war that began in February 2022. Witkoff said Ukraine and Russia had agreed to a three-day ceasefire before their visit to the region following months without significant progress toward a peace agreement. The ceasefire ended on Tuesday. KUSHNER, WITKOFF SET FOR KYIV TALKS AFTER PUTIN MEETING IN US PUSH FOR PEACE "Substantive progress was made, including movement on scheduling additional trilateral talks. President Trump is working hard to stop the killing and work towards a lasting and durable peace," he wrote on X following the trip. On Tuesday morning, the governor of the Russian city of Saratov said a Ukrainian drone struck civilian infrastructure and injured some people. Russian attacks killed multiple people and wounded dozens of others across Ukraine over the past day, Ukrainian officials said on Monday. Additionally, Ukrainian drones struck three Russian oil refineries on Monday.
title: Russian strikes continue following visit by Witkoff and Kushner to Kyiv
author: Fox News

content: The United Kingdom is expected to announce restrictions targeting trade with Israeli settlements in the West Bank on Tuesday, a move already drawing strong pushback Monday from U.S. and Israeli officials. According to The Times , a US State Department said Washington was "tracking the plans closely." The measures are expected to include an embargo on goods and some services involving West Bank settlements marking an escalation in London’s pressure on Israel under new Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has taken a firmer stance on the conflict, according to reports . The announcement is expected to come a day after Burnham spoke by phone with President Donald Trump. WHO IS ANDY BURNHAM? BRITAIN'S NEW PRIME MINISTER AND LONGTIME TRUMP CRITIC According to a No. 10 Downing Street readout of the call Monday, the two leaders discussed the Middle East, with Burnham highlighting the importance of a two-state solution which calls for an independent Palestinian state comprising the West Bank and Gaza Strip to exist alongside Israel. "On the Middle East, the Prime Minister set out the UK’s commitment to working towards peace and security in the region, stressing the importance of the Two-State Solution," the spokesperson said. The readout did not mention the planned sanctions. Bloomberg reported, however, that the timing of the call suggested Burnham may have briefed Trump on the measures targeting goods and services linked to Israeli settlements in the West Bank. The move could create an early point of friction between Burnham and Washington , where the Trump administration has strongly backed Israel, the outlet said. I’M AN ARAB MUSLIM — I STILL DON’T UNDERSTAND THE ANTISEMITIC BDS MOVEMENT The new measures, billed widely as sanctions, are expected to be formally unveiled by Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband, who has already pledged a " comprehensive reset " of Britain’s policy toward Israeli settlements in the West Bank. Miliband signaled last week that measures were coming in response to Israeli settlement expansion, including the E1 project east of Jerusalem, according to The National . He went on to describe E1 as a longstanding "red line" and said Britain would take action to protect the prospect of a two-state solution. The planned sanction announcement has already drawn sharp criticism in Israel and the United States. Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich called for the British ambassador’s expulsion in a post on X. "We will not be a doormat for an antisemitic government in a country occupied by radical Islam that is trying to escape economic and social collapse by attacking Jews and the State of Israel," Smotrich wrote. "The British Mandate in Israel is over." EX-PENTAGON OFFICIAL URGES US TO ‘SQUEEZE’ UK ON DEFENSE AMID FALKLANDS FUROR National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir also condemned the planned restrictions, writing in Spanish on X that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu should retaliate by recognizing Argentine sovereignty over th
title: UK moves to sanction Israeli settlements as PM Burnham risks clash with Trump: report
author: Fox News

content: Israeli Ambassador to the United Nations Danny Danon told Fox News Digital that New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is "sowing chaos" ahead of Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s visit to the U.N. General Assembly later this month. Danon made the remark after Mamdani called on New Yorkers in July to protest when Netanyahu arrives to speak at the general debate at U.N. headquarters on Sept. 24. "No one can ignore Mayor Mamdani, you know, instead of actually welcoming all world leaders and making sure that the city will function properly, he is doing exactly the opposite," Danon said. "He is inciting, he is sowing chaos into the city. So this year, unfortunately, it will be harder for every New Yorker or every visitor because the mayor is actually calling for people to go out, to demonstrate and it will not deter us. The prime minister will come, will speak and will represent our nation," the ambassador added. ISRAELI PM BENJAMIN NETANYAHU VOWS TO VISIT NEW YORK DESPITE MAMDANI'S REPEATED CALLS FOR HIS ARREST Mamdani’s office, when asked by Fox News Digital if he had any plans to meet with Netanyahu while he is in town, did not immediately respond to a request for comment. "I don't think the prime minister wants to meet with him," Danon said. Mamdani previously called Netanyahu a "war criminal" and "architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people." The Democratic socialist also acknowledged that he can't have Netanyahu arrested despite promising to do so during his mayoral campaign. When asked by a reporter in July about "What do you think that these people who are frustrated with Netanyahu should do when he arrives in New York City for the United Nations meeting," Mamdani said, "One of the bedrocks of our city is protest." "It is something that has been a part of what makes our city so special, that New Yorkers can express themselves whether they are in support or in opposition no matter on whatever topic," the Democratic socialist mayor said during the press conference on July 22. "And I’ve always said that when we respect our Constitution, we also respect our First Amendment. And here in New York City it will always be a place where you can exercise that." IRAN TRIED TO ASSASSINATE ONE OF NETANYAHU'S SONS, PRIME MINISTER SAYS Netanyahu told Fox News "Hannity" around a week later that, "I’m going to New York," and, "I'm going to speak the truth in front of this hate-spewing elected official who's pitting one group of New Yorkers against the others." Danon told Fox News Digital that "we have been involved in a war, a difficult one, a long one, and I think now we have a lot of opportunities ahead of us." "So the prime minister would also speak about what we achieved, but also about the opportunities," he said. Danon also said Israel has to "finish the job" in Gaza. "Hamas is still there. They are supposed to disarm, according to the president's plan. I hope it will take place. I hope that it will happen sooner than later beca
title: Israel's ambassador says NYC’s Mamdani is ‘sowing chaos’ ahead of Netanyahu’s UN appearance
author: Fox Politics

content: Hasan Piker hears the growing chorus of Democrats condemning him for incendiary statements, and he has a message for the party: "My job is not to make the Democratic Party look good." The far-left Twitch streamer has boosted socialist candidates even as he created headaches for the broader Democratic Party in a midterm election cycle where it hopes to make major gains. The 35-year-old Piker — whose polarizing stances range from defending communist Chinese dictator Mao Zedong to comparing Zionism to "Nazism" — is a darling of the Democratic Socialists of America, but a potential liability for mainstream Democrats as November approaches. Piker said Democratic Party officials have not reached out to coordinate a strategy. "I have not had a conversation with anyone from the DNC," Piker said. "That would be very funny." JAMES CARVILLE DECRIES 'IDIOT' HASAN PIKER, ORDERS DSA TO CHANGE ITS NAME In an exclusive interview at the 2026 Socialism Conference in Chicago, Piker told Fox News that, while he tries "to be as careful as possible" when it comes to choosing his words, his hours-long streams present his opponents with the "perfect opportunity to create viral media moments." Some of those moments include intense backlash over Piker’s 2019 statement that America "deserved 9/11," a comment which has been widely condemned by politicians on both sides of the aisle. HASAN PIKER CALLS REPUBLICAN PARTY THE 'BIGGEST DOMESTIC TERRORIST' IN THE COUNTRY Piker acknowledged that he should not have used the word "deserved," but said his point was that "[America’s] meddling in the affairs in the Middle East actually transpired these horrifying events." "It's not a controversial thing [to argue]," Piker said. "It was the language that I used that was controversial." HASAN PIKER CALLS HAMAS 'FAR MORE MODERATE,' DISMISSES TERROR GROUP’S BRUTAL RULE IN GAZA Piker's brash commentary gives him credence with the far-left DSA , which pulled off a host of primary victories against more moderate Democrats, but party elders have disavowed him. "There’s two things that I know about Hasan Piker," longtime Democratic Party consultant James Carville told Fox News Channel last week. "One, he’s an idiot, and two, he’s not a Democrat. So, I don’t answer for idiots, and I don’t answer for people who are not Democrats." VAN JONES WARNS FAR-LEFT SOCIALIST AGENDA IS 'REGRESSIVE' THREAT TO DEMOCRATIC PARTY Key Democrat lawmakers, including House Minority Leader Hakeen Jeffries, senators Cory Booker , D-N.J., and Jon Ossoff, D-Ga., and several House members have condemned Piker's past rhetoric. As he crosses the country, joining campaign rallies and canvass launches for liberal challengers to establishment-backed candidates, Piker acknowledged that even his allies have urged him to moderate his rhetoric for the sake of their electoral chances. DEMOCRATS' CIVIL WAR HEADS TO MICHIGAN WHERE PROGRESSIVES FACE BIGGEST TEST YET IN HIGH-STAKES SENATE SHOWDOWN But Piker told Fox News the press is o
title: Hasan Piker brushes off Dems who see him as a liability, names his '28 choice
author: Fox Politics

content: Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed is seeking to appear more moderate to voters while, at the same time, maintaining ties to individuals who take positions far to the left of anything he publicly endorses. Since launching his Senate bid in April 2025, El-Sayed has distanced himself from a number of positions he had previously held and scrubbed much of his left-wing pre-campaign content from the internet. He has also repeatedly insisted that he is "not a socialist." While attempting to convince voters that characterizations of him as a left-wing ideologue are inaccurate, El-Sayed has appeared at campaign events with and accepted endorsements from a range of political allies and supporters with controversial records or views. EL-SAYED’S HASAN PIKER PROBLEM FOLLOWS HIM TO DEM CONVENTION AS JEWISH VOTERS BREAK RANKS Beyond campaigning with Twitch streamer Hasan Piker , who claimed that America "deserved" 9/11, El-Sayed has also linked himself with terror-sympathetic Islamic clerics, individuals accused of antisemitism and several prominent socialists and socialist-aligned activists. "Abdul has made clear that no one speaks for his campaign besides himself and his campaign spokespeople," El-Sayed campaign spokesman Cole Wozniak told Fox News Digital. El-Sayed's campaign has attempted to flip the narrative on Republicans, pointing out that Mike Rogers, the GOP nominee facing off against him, has his own set of controversial associations. Some individuals affiliated with the Rogers campaign, which did not respond to a request for comment, have also cast doubt on the outcome of the 2020 election and advocated for banning gay marriage. Nonetheless, Republicans have made El-Sayed's affiliations with controversial figures a focal point of their campaign in Michigan. "I am not somebody who is a socialist," El-Sayed told CNN in July. "I believe in capitalism, I just believe that capitalism has to be regulated." Despite this assertion, and multiple others like it, El-Sayed has surrounded himself with socialists during his tenure as a public figure. Sen. Bernie Sanders , an independent from Vermont described by some as the avatar of socialism in America, threw his support behind El-Sayed’s ill-fated 2018 gubernatorial run. The Vermont socialist was also among the first to back El-Sayed’s 2026 Senate bid , endorsing him on the same day he launched his campaign. Sanders isn’t the only socialist backing El-Sayed’s run for Senate. Reps. Rashida Tlaib, Summer Lee and Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez are all vocal supporters. TOP DEM HOPEFUL FLIPS SCRIPT AFTER YEARS IN SOCIALIST ORBIT WITH PUZZLING CLAIM El-Sayed has long aligned himself with the Democratic Socialists of America , only recently distancing himself from the ascendant left-wing organization as he seeks to win a competitive Senate race. Between 2017 and 2020, the Michigan Democrat spoke at six events held by Democratic Socialists of America chapters, including a 2019 fundraiser where he served a
title: ‘Destroying the American way of life’: El-Sayed’s political orbit complicates effort to moderate his image

content: Republicans and Democrats across Capitol Hill are getting a glimpse of artificial intelligence’s latest power: its ability to churn out instant dossiers filled with details about ordinary Americans, from a gun store owner’s leaked email passwords to a church member’s yoga workouts to people's visits to abortion clinics. And it’s freaking them out. Lawmakers and staffers from dozens of congressional offices have seen AI’s privacy-busting prowess in demos arranged in recent months by CivAI, a nonprofit that says its aim is to educate the public about AI's dangers and capabilities. Besides building troves of personal information gleaned from commercial databases, the dossiers offer advice on potential ways to blackmail, coerce or stalk the individual in question, according to four Republican and eight Democratic staffers who were granted anonymity because they were not authorized to speak on the record. The demos started landing amid the debate over whether to renew a set of government spying powers that expired in June — legislation that offers the most realistic chance for addressing the issue during this Congress, a Democratic House aide who witnessed one of the briefings said. While commercial databases have long made it possible to purchase information on people’s travels, shopping habits, subscriptions, employment histories and social media profiles, AI makes it easier to quickly pull that data into one place — and to build detailed profiles about virtually any American who owns a phone. The technology adds to long-standing concerns from some lawmakers about federal agencies buying this kind of data on U.S. citizens without obtaining a warrant. “Today, anyone with access to a frontier AI model can buy your data from a broker and reconstruct an intimate picture of your life, including your location, your purchases, your browsing history, and even who you love or where you worship,” Rep. Lori Trahan (D-Mass.) said in a statement. “CivAI's work showing members and staff exactly how easy this is should be a wake-up call for Congress, which has spent years failing to act.” Despite the typically bleak prospects for strong privacy laws on Capitol Hill, the demos were effective at introducing the issue to congressional offices not steeped in tech policy, staffers said, thanks in part to the briefings' focus on potential harms to voters such as gun owners, activists or people seeking abortions. "It made clear that our constitutional and statutory privacy protections have not kept pace with modern technology," said a Republican House staffer who saw one of the demos in July. “Congress needs to act before AI and the unchecked commercial sale of personal data erode the privacy protections Americans have relied on for generations.” 'Find church-going Christians in Janesville, Wisconsin’ The dozen staffers who spoke to POLITICO work for lawmakers spanning the ideological spectrum, including members of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, Artificial Intelli
title: Own a gun? Go to church? Do yoga? AI can find out in seconds.
author: Alfred Ng

content: Democratic Senate candidate Angie Nixon visits Miami’s Little Havana neighborhood as she campaigns on August 29, 2026. | Joe Raedle/Getty Images Last month, Florida state Rep. Angie Nixon won the state’s Democratic Senate nomination in a major upset over her better-funded opponent, retired Army Lt. Col. Alex Vindman. Her victory was quickly slotted into a narrative about the Democratic Party’s insurgent progressive movement, which has triumphed in House and Senate primaries in Michigan, Colorado, New York, and elsewhere. But while Nixon supports progressive policies, she argues there’s more to the story than a simple progressive-versus-centrist tale. She says that she out-worked and out-organized her opponent — and that Floridians across the political spectrum are hungry for change.  Vox’s Astead Herndon invited Nixon on a special pop-up episode of America, Actually to break down how she won the nomination, why she thinks there’s a path to victory in what many analysts believe is a solidly red state , and what she wants to get done as a senator if she prevails in November. Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity. There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel . Why do you think your victory took so many by surprise? It took so many by surprise because people both tend to underestimate a Black woman — especially a progressive Black woman in politics — and then one who wasn’t able to raise as much money. But as a former single mom for 12 years, I know how to make a dollar stretch. This win is attributed to good old-fashioned grassroots organizing. I am a former union organizer. I am a community organizer, and I know the importance of people power and talking to people and getting them energized about why they should vote and why they should see themselves in this country. How much would you ascribe your win to the type of politics that you’re describing here versus the progressive policies that you championed? Should we take this as a sign that Medicare-for-all and “abolish ICE” have strong support in Florida? It’s all of it, right? It is the hard work that we put into this race to raise awareness about who I am and the policies and positions that I stand for, which are policies and positions that the majority of hardworking, everyday people stand for.  Just because we want access to quality healthcare and affordable housing and fully funded public schools, they try to fear-monger and make it seem as though we are communist and we’re not. We are not communist. We are people who want to put hardworking, everyday people in power so that they can determine and shape what our communities look like and what our economies look like. There’s nothing radical or extreme about that. Democrats are still dismissing your chances to win a general election. Prominent pundits have said that Democrats shoul
title: Can Democrats flip Florida in 2026?
author: Astead Herndon

content: Abdul El-Sayed, US Democratic Senate candidate from Michigan, leaves the stage after speaking during the state Democratic Party's nominating convention on August 29, 2026 in Lansing, Michigan. | Sara Rice/Bloomberg via Getty Images Abdul El-Sayed is trying to win over undecided Jewish voters in Michigan — without compromising his substantive positions on Israel or disavowing his most radical allies.   During both his primary and general election campaigns, El-Sayed’s opponents have portrayed him as insensitive to Jewish concerns, if not outright antisemitic . These charges have often rested on falsely equating El-Sayed’s opposition to Zionism (he is not committed to Israel’s existence as a majority Jewish state) with a hostility for Jewish people. But in recent weeks, two other concerns came to the forefront. One was El-Sayed’s response to an antisemitic attack on a Michigan synagogue. In March, a 41-year-old named Ayman Mohamed Ghazali drove a truck into Temple Israel’s Jewish preschool. Days later, El-Sayed condemned the attack, while also noting that Ghazali had recently lost family members to an Israeli airstrike in Lebanon. El-Sayed suggested that these events illustrated how “hurt people hurt people” and that “violence is a cycle,” one that had led Ghazali to perpetrate “an evil act of displaced rage.” Separately, El-Sayed had campaigned with the far-left streamer Hasan Piker during his primary campaign. This had always sat poorly with many Jewish and centrist Democrats in Michigan. But Piker made his association with the Democratic Senate candidate more conspicuous in late August. During a broadcast, Piker lambasted Jeremy Moss , a pro-Israel Jewish Democrat running for Congress in Michigan who had not endorsed El-Sayed but was in active conversations with the candidate about how to bridge lingering divides with Jewish voters . More explosively, Piker said, among other things, that “if Jews in America keep putting this idea out there that they are singularly invested in Israel, eventually somebody is going to come around and take action, not against the State of Israel, mind you, but against American Jews.” He subsequently insisted he was merely spotlighting the hazards of portraying all Jews as ardent Israel supporters, not making some kind of veiled threat, as his detractors alleged. Nonetheless, this triggered a new round of calls for El-Sayed to both disavow Piker, and to take other measures to reassure Michigan Jews that he cares about their safety.  These disagreements between El-Sayed and moderate Jewish voters reflect broader tensions within the Democratic Party nationally. El-Sayed declined to disown the streamer. But he did defend the right of all Americans “to advocate for what they believe without fear of violence,” saying this was “particularly true for communities that have been intimidated for their beliefs in the past.” Some Jewish Democrats found this insufficient. In an open letter Wednesday, 400 Democratic
title: The Jewish Democrats trying to get to “yes” on Abdul El-Sayed
author: Eric Levitz

content: A quarter century after the September 11 attacks emboldened then-President George W. Bush to launch the “ war on terror ,” many Americans might like to think they’re wiser than the politicians and pundits who unleashed a flood of anti-Muslim hatred and eroded civil liberties through warrantless wiretaps and racist deportation campaigns . But some of the most notorious Bush-era advents — like the Department of Homeland Security and the prison colony at Guantánamo Bay — don’t appear to be going anywhere. Nor does the phenomenon of Islamophobia, which is playing a major role in the current political cycle. Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed — who, if elected, would be the first Muslim U.S. senator — has been called a terrorist, a radical Islamist, and a threat to national security, as pro-corporate and pro-Israel super PACs spend millions on ads that paint him as a terrorist sympathizer . In New York City, meanwhile, local media has suggested that the city’s first Muslim mayor, Zohran Mamdani, should not attend the commemoration of the World Trade Center attacks, as if to do so would be an insult to the victims and their families. “Islamophobia actually becomes more rampant during election season — not necessarily after a terrorist attack, but actually during election season in the U.S.,” journalist Rozina Ali tells The Intercept Briefing. “What’s happened over the last three decades is that Islamophobia has become a feature of American politics. … When you can’t actually discuss the policies, when we’re not willing to engage in facts, it’s really easy to throw racist rhetoric at people.” “The fight that we’re seeing now is whether we are willing to accept all forms of religion in this country. And as much as I want to say this is just more of what we’ve seen in the past, I think what does frighten me is how quickly we are moving to a place where some governor or some local official might try to outlaw Islam altogether. And mind you, this is even a policy shift from 10 years ago when Trump called for a Muslim ban,” says Ali. “What has been happening recently is that the rhetoric … has been shifting toward, ‘Islam is not a religion, it’s a political ideology.’ This is not a new talking point, but it is becoming institutionalized. There are efforts to make it into law, which is a frightening place to be.” This week on the podcast, host Akela Lacy speaks to Ali about how anti-Muslim rhetoric and policies are on the rise and have endured, or even worsened, in the post-9/11 world, as well as her new book , “Seasons of Fury: Four Families and the Rise of Islamophobia in America.” Ali shares the first case in which the NSA admitted to spying on a U.S. citizen, Arab American attorney Abdeen Jabara, as well as the story of imam Yassin Aref, a victim of a controversial sting operation who served 15 years in federal prison due to the ambiguous “material support” for terrorism law first passed
title: 25 Years After 9/11, Muslims Are Still Politicians’ Favorite Scapegoat
author: The Intercept Briefing

content: Marc Rowan has a vision for Gaza. “The potential here is tremendous,” he said at a February gathering of President Donald Trump’s so-called Board of Peace, where Rowan described land devastated by Israeli bombing with a developer’s zeal. “This is not a problem of money or collateral. This is a problem with peace.” In the U.S., Rowan is simultaneously helping ensure a pro-Israel political project has no problem with money. Since the start of this year, according to Federal Election Commission filings, the billionaire CEO of Apollo Global Management has donated $1.5 million to the United Democracy Project, a super PAC for the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, spending a fraction of his vast wealth to preserve a foreign policy defined by support for Israel’s genocide and the flow of U.S. weapons to Israel.  “Palestinians did not choose him, and neither did American voters.” Rowan — who is worth more than $8 billion and reportedly consulted on his business with convicted sex offender and disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein — is an executive member of Trump’s “Board of Peace,” a United Nations-approved body tasked with carrying out Trump’s stalled plan for Gaza. He made his first donation to UDP of the year in early March, giving $1 million, filings show, just as the group began spending aggressively against the now-ousted Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., a loud critic of U.S. support for Israel .  A second donation for $500,000 arrived on July 23. The same day, the AIPAC super PAC shelled out nearly $50,000 in campaign mailers in Michigan to attack the progressive pro-Palestine candidate for U.S. Senate, Abdul El-Sayed. In Missouri, it dropped another $100,000 for phone banking services against former Democratic Rep. Cori Bush in her race against pro-Israel incumbent Rep. Wesley Bell.  Related AIPAC, AI, Crypto, and Gambling Are Hiding Their Big Election Spends It’s not clear which specific UDP efforts have been backed by Rowan’s largesse, and neither Rowan nor UDP responded to requests for comment. But Raed Jarrar, advocacy director with Democracy for the Arab World Now , connected Rowan’s position on Trump’s Gaza board and his major part as a donor to AIPAC’s super PAC as a matter of transparency.  “Now he sits on a board that will decide Gaza’s future,” Jarrar told The Intercept. “Palestinians did not choose him, and neither did American voters. Americans and Palestinians alike deserve to know whose interests are actually being served.” Rowan, a major donor to Trump’s failed 2020 presidential campaign, has long made his animus toward critics of Israel known. In recent years, he has been a fierce advocate against student protesters calling for an end to the genocide in Gaza, broadly mischaracterizing their anti-genocide calls as “antisemitic,” and played a key role in ousting leaders at his alma mater , the University of Pennsylvania, over thei

content: Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks with reporters at the Michigan Theatre in Ann Arbor, Mich., on Aug. 26, 2026.   Photo: Jeff Kowalsky/AFP via Getty Images It always felt inevitable that Bari Weiss’s tenure at CBS News would see the network devolve into rank Islamophobia — but even for most of us, who took a dim view of her takeover of the news behemoth, tying Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed to the 9/11 attacks was an unexpected new low. To make matters worse, many centrist Democrats and their allies cleared the way for just this kind of attack. On Monday, CBS reporter Zak Hudak published an article headlined with the critique that El-Sayed’s “deleted tweets on Sept. 11 attacks invite scrutiny of past remarks.” Weiss, whose time in charge of CBS has been rife with controversy , was reportedly deeply involved with the story’s promotion and framing, going so far as to praise it in a newsroom meeting and champion it “to the entire network,” according to media-industry newsletter Status . She “even personally directed the headline to be tweaked to specifically mention” the 9/11 angle. The story immediately came under harsh criticism, even from people whose politics when it comes to Muslims are virtually indistinguishable from Weiss’s. Atlantic writer Jonathan Chait, for example, called the tweets a “non-story.” Related 3,000 Dead on 9/11 Meant Everything. 200,000 Dead of Covid-19 Means Nothing. Here’s Why. CBS declined to mention that two of those three deleted posts were asking Americans to take the death toll of the Covid-19 pandemic as seriously as the attacks. It’s worth noting — CBS did not — that invoking 9/11 to put the Covid death toll in perspective wasn’t unusual at the time; then-Gov. Andrew Cuomo directly compared the pandemic, which ravaged New York City, to the attacks the same month that El-Sayed did. Another post at issue was a rather anodyne comment about the consequences of the decadelong war on terror and a call to action: “We could save lives rather than take them.” El-Sayed’s campaign previously told Politico that all posts older than July 2023 were deleted “to prevent any old posts from being taken out of context.” Weiss’s guidance led to CBS News’s racist framing that there’s just something different — even untrustworthy — about El-Sayed, and that the upcoming 25th anniversary of 9/11 is the right time to ask what that is. In doing so, she’s embracing a long-standing bipartisan tradition of Muslim dehumanization — a playbook still being deployed on both sides of the aisle. The current anti-Muslim environment reflects the growth and regression in the country since the 9/11 moment: growth in the number of Muslims in political and public life, and the regressive backlash to multicultural liberalism that’s defined the Trump era. Related How Democrats Paved the Way for Kevin McCarthy’s Attack on Ilhan Omar This kind of bigotry was rampant during the early 2000s , p
title: CBS News Spins El-Sayed’s 9/11 Tweets Into a Manufactured Anti-Muslim Scandal
author: Eoin Higgins

content: “We won,” ‌ President Donald Trump declared in March, less than two weeks after launching his war of choice against Iran. Claiming that nation was “very much destroyed and, even, obliterated,” Trump had already promised the conflict would bring peace to the region and, somehow, the globe. “The heavy and pinpoint bombing … will continue, uninterrupted … as long as necessary to achieve our objective of PEACE THROUGHOUT THE MIDDLE EAST AND, INDEED, THE WORLD!” Trump wrote . But more than six months and two failed ceasefires later, the floundering conflict sputters along. And you may have noticed that world peace has yet to be announced. Having again been bested in battle — the latest loss in a long-running series of meaningless victories (like over lowly Grenada), stalemates (like the forever war in Somalia ), and defeats (like conflicts in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia) — the U.S. military has slunk away from the fight in favor of an “economic D-Day” that so far seems to be little more than bluster. Trump’s other stated war aims, like Iran’s unconditional surrender and seizing its oil infrastructure, have also fallen by the wayside. In the end, the major accomplishments of Trump’s war seem to be limited to death and destruction: hundreds of U.S. casualties that the Pentagon has sought to downplay and cover-up , and thousands of Iranian deaths that the Pentagon is loath to mention or investigate , including a family of eight — five of them children, one a 20-day-old infant . But the almost 40,000 Iranians killed or wounded in the war may only scratch the surface of the true toll, as Ashley Gate writes in her latest piece for TomDispatch. The rough outlines of the ecological devastation are only just coming to light. And if history is any guide, the environmental fallout of the war may reach far into the future, affecting untold numbers of Iranians who survived the conflict and many others in generations to come. — Nick Turse, editor of TomDispatch If you haven’t yet, sign up to receive TomDispatch in your inbox here. The Toxic Inheritance of America’s Wars Esmaeil Baqaei, the spokesperson for Iran’s Foreign Ministry, recently warned of the increasing environmental damage caused by the U.S. war, drawing attention to oil contamination in the Persian Gulf that has begun washing up on Iranian shores. “This incident is only one visible example of the extensive pollution — both overt and concealed — that has degraded the waters of the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman,” he wrote on X. “Who bears responsibility for compensating these damages? Is it the nations that consume the inexpensive energy exported from our region, the shipping insurers, or the aggressors and their partners who have transformed the Persian Gulf and the Sea of Oman into a theater for military operations and the testing of highly destructive weaponry?” Alongside death and destruction that has killed or wounded tens of thousands of Iranians, the U.S.–Israeli war has caused massive environm
title: Ecocide in Iran
author: Ashley Gate

content: When police in Kent, United Kingdom, arrested American peace activist Max Geller in 2021 for chaining himself to a van parked in front of an Israeli-owned weapons factory, he knew he might be jailed and face charges for his protest.  What he didn’t realize was that he could be hit with U.S. sanctions five years later for his past ties to a so-called terrorist organization.  The Trump administration on Wednesday announced sanctions against the U.K.-based anti-genocide protest group Palestine Action , which organized the 2021 demonstration and dozens of subsequent actions at U.K. factories owned by Israel’s largest weapons manufacturer, Elbit Systems. The goal, in the U.S. government’s words, is to “protect Americans from the risks posed by far-left terrorism.” “A major threshold has been crossed,” said Geller, who was previously Palestine Action’s spokesperson but left the group in 2025, when the British government made membership punishable by 14 years in prison. “They’re now treating regular Americans who want to effectively oppose genocide as terrorists.” The specific parameters of the U.S. sanctions are not yet clear, but Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent pledged the government would “continue to cut the financial lifelines of these groups until they are eliminated.” Sanctioned groups and individuals cannot receive funds, goods, or services from American people or business — meaning they’re cut off from both the U.S. banking system and from any donations from Americans who might want to support them. They can have an isolating global effect: Financial institutions outside the U.S. that do business with American companies are often hesitant to affiliate with sanctioned individuals. As a result, the sanctions could severely curtail their organizing abilities — and restrict their ability to try to stop the flow of weapons that Israel is using to carry out its ongoing genocide in Gaza. “We are facing unprecedented attacks on dissent by the same powers that are committing genocide in Gaza,” said Huda Ammori, co-founder of Palestine Action, in an interview with The Intercept. “We are at a point in history where it’s extremely crucial to continue to resist and grow in our movement, rather than back down and to adapt and become less reliant on institutions which are essentially controlled by the powers we’re fighting against.”  Related They Weren’t Convicted of Terrorism, But These Palestine Activists Got Sentenced as Terrorists Anyway While the new U.S. sanctions are a part of a long history of post-9/11 policies in its so-called war on terror, the U.K. government has made itself notorious for its specific draconian crackdown on pro-Palestine dissent. Last year, as Palestine Action members began to face terror charges in court for their demonstrations, the U.K. government proscribed the group as a terrorist organization. The organization in the U.K. immediately ceased operations after the terror proscription. Dozens of members in the U.
title: “They Want People Scared”: Former Palestine Action Member Blasts Trump’s Terror Sanctions
author: Jonah Valdez

content: Our previous work examined the forces creating fiscal pressure on higher education, the divide between “Elites” and “Pragmatics,” and whether pursuing a degree makes financial sense . This is Part IV, about making prudent choices if one decides to pursue higher education. Colleges and the media have applauded the surge of underprepared students entering college, often treating capability and merit as though they should play little or no role in admission. They call this expansion “ inclusion” and “ equal access,” cheering as though the doors of an exclusive country club have finally been thrown open to those long denied entry. Perhaps if colleges were required to cosign the loans their students take out to pay soaring tuition, they would view this trend differently. Millions of Americans have been left with student-loan debt that can hamstring them for decades, even after earning a diploma. For some, college was the worst financial decision they ever made. This does not mean a degree is always a bad choice. It means the decision should be made analytically, with a clear understanding of both its potential benefits and risks. Finding Your Passion At most universities, students are encouraged to “ find their passion,” as if it is a mystical creature that, once discovered, will automatically produce a fun, effortless education and a high-paying career. This advice often comes with several other misconceptions. Students may be led to believe that studying something they love will never feel like work, that passion is innate rather than developed, or that difficulty with a subject means they have chosen the wrong field. They may also assume that pursuing a passion will automatically lead to a well-paying career because the success stories most often reported reinforce that impression. The “ find your passion” trope can distract students from considerations with far greater consequences for their financial futures. Many articles, often promoted by colleges themselves, emphasize the lifetime earnings difference between people with and without degrees. That generalization may hold on average, but it obscures an important reality: not all college degrees produce the same economic return. Students are too often given the impression that their prospects will be essentially indistinguishable whether their “ passion” is recreational sports management or chemical engineering — as long as it produces a degree. Employment data tell us otherwise. With the proliferation of majors and the soaring cost of higher education, choosing the right major has become more important than ever. The earnings premium associated with a degree is not guaranteed and may be surprisingly small or nonexistent for some. Graduation is the beginning of a career journey, not its destination. Selecting a major should therefore involve more than identifying a student ’ s interests. It should also assess the time and money required to earn the degree and whether that
title: Rethinking College: Choose The Path, Not Just The Degree
author: Greg Salsbury and John Kawauchi

content: We moved into a new house this week. I had forgotten to call ahead and arrange internet service before moving day, and when I finally applied, I was told the earliest installation date was ten days away. Both my wife’s work and mine depend almost entirely on being online. Our phone hotspots burned through their data almost immediately, so I texted our next-door neighbor, a white American Christian whom I had spoken with only briefly. I explained the situation and asked whether we could use his Wi-Fi until ours was installed. As a thank-you, I offered to pay his internet bill for the month. He apologized and said no. As someone who grew up as a Muslim in the Islamic world, lived in several Muslim countries, and traveled to perhaps twenty more, I can say with confidence that I would be surprised to find a Muslim who would refuse that request from a new neighbor. When I was ten years old, I lived in Jerash, Jordan, a city filled with Roman ruins because ancient Gerasa was one of the cities of the Decapolis. We saw tourists constantly. I still remember an Italian tourist who seemed lost. I found him a cab, explained where he needed to go, and paid the entire fare out of the small allowance I had, even though no one expected me to. Hospitality was simply something we were taught to do. I doubt many cultures can compete with Arabs and Muslims when it comes to hospitality. Knock on the door of a Muslim family and, before they ask why you have come, there is a good chance they will invite you inside, offer you food and something to drink, and only then ask what brought you there. Stop a Muslim on the street and ask for help, and he will never brush you off the way people often do in the West. He may spend an hour with you if that is what it takes to make sure you find what you need. Last week, during the CAIR summit, several speakers talked about the need for Muslims to spend more time with Americans so that Americans could see how nice Muslims are and thereby combat what they described as “Islamophobia.” I can see why they think that strategy will work. Last year, I was invited to speak at a synagogue about Islam. Afterward, a Jewish woman objected to what I had said because, as she explained, her daughter had a very nice Muslim friend. This is where many people in the West become confused. They hear Muslim clerics speak about Islam’s global ambitions, they see what Muslim terrorists do around the world, they remember the beheadings, the persecution of minorities, the grooming and rape gangs, and other acts committed by Muslims. At the same time, they personally know Muslims who are kind, generous, decent people. Faced with that contradiction, many resolve it by separating the Islam of their nice Muslim friends from the actions of violent Muslims and treating the latter as a fringe phenomenon with little or nothing to do with Islam itself. When a Muslim man stopped two ISIS terrorists in Sydney, his religion was immediately emphasized. He was not “the h
title: The Conflation Of Muslim And Islamic Could Be The End Of The West
author: Danny Burmawi

content: A Jewish advocacy group is demanding Ed Sheeran fire Macklemore as his opening act, accusing the rapper of hijacking two MetLife stadium shows to deliver anti-Israel messaging the group says amounts to antisemitic propaganda. The Israeli-American Council launched a petition Sunday calling for the “Thrift Shop” rapper’s removal from the remainder of Sheeran’s “Loop Tour.” Macklemore, born Benjamin Haggerty, performed as an opener at the East Rutherford, New Jersey, stadium on Friday and Saturday nights, telling the crowd of more than 80,000 that he wanted people in Gaza and the West Bank to know “they had not been forgotten” before leading chants of “Free Palestine.” Wearing a keffiyeh over his shoulders, he then performed his 2024 protest song, “Hind’s Hall,” while images from Gaza and pro-Palestinian campus encampments played on the stadium’s video screens. Macklemore’s last major moment of mainstream attention prior to his post-October 7 activism came with 2012’s “Same Love,” a song in which he recounted believing as a child that he might be gay. “Hind’s Hall” takes its name from the moniker stadium demonstrators gave Columbia University’s Hamilton Hall after occupying the building during 2024 campus protests, and from Hind Rajab, a young Palestinian girl killed in Gaza. The IAC’s petition argues the song choice was “not incidental,” noting that some of the campus unrest it commemorates involved trespassing, building takeovers and vandalism. “This was an Ed Sheeran concert – not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event,” the petition states, adding that “freedom of expression does not mean freedom from responsibility.” The group, which says it represents more than 150,000 Israeli-Americans and belongs to the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations, addressed its petition to Sheeran, his tour management, upcoming tour venues and promoter Live Nation. The advocacy group StopAntisemitism amplified the controversy on X, posting video of the performance and writing that “Jewish patrons should not be subjected to this propaganda.” The group also revived criticism of an earlier Macklemore bit in which the he appeared onstage dressed as an Orthodox Jew with an exaggerated prosthetic nose, calling on the rapper to issue “apologies and refunds” to fans. Here we go again – despite massive backlash surrounding Macklemore opening for @edsheeran , a repeat occurred a few moments ago at @MetLifeStadium in New Jersey. Jewish patrons should not be subjected to this propaganda. pic.twitter.com/dRvFkHWA2T — StopAntisemitism (@StopAntisemites) September 6, 2026 As of publication, Sheeran had not publicly responded, and Macklemore remains listed as an opener for the tour’s upcoming dates. title: Long-Forgotten Rapper Hijacks Ed Sheeran Concert With Bizarre Islamist Propaganda

content: This story was originally published by  The Guardian   and is reproduced here as part of the  Climate Desk   collaboration. Almost half of the world’s farmers are poisoned by pesticides every single year, a  study  has found. Using publicly available data from 2006-2023, the study, which was commissioned by  Pesticide Action Network , found there to be an estimated 402 million to 433 million cases of unintentional acute pesticide poisoning of farmers and farm workers every year. Based on a worldwide farming population of 934 million, this means approximately 46 percent of farmers are being poisoned every year. The greatest estimated number of poisonings was in southern Asia, followed by Southeast Asia and East  Africa . The overall highest national incidence of poisoning was in  Burkina Faso  in West Africa, where nearly 84 percent of farmers and farm workers were reported to have experienced poisoning. The study,  published  in the journal Frontiers in Public Health this past Wednesday, also found that an estimated 11,000 deaths occur every year due to pesticide poisoning, with nearly 60 percent of these in India. The director general of Parkinson’s Europe said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease. Jayakumar Chelaton, the executive director of Pesticide Action Network  India , said the research exposed a “crisis that can no longer be ignored.” The authors of the study are calling for “immediate action,” including the implementation of a UN recommendation to phase out highly hazardous pesticides. The study states that despite global efforts to highlight the dangers, pesticide use has continued to grow steadily, with 3.8 million metric tons used in 2023, a doubling since 1990. Dr Sheila Willis, the head of international programmes at Pesticide Action Network UK, said: “Now that the scale of suffering has been revealed, farmers must be supported to access safer alternatives to protect their health and that of their families.” The study did not consider the impact of pesticide exposure on the estimated 84 million children working in agriculture and did not look at the long-term health impacts, with acute pesticide poisoning defined in the study as any illness or health effect experienced a short time after exposure. Génon Jensen, the executive director of the  Health  and Environment Alliance, said: “We are extremely concerned about the devastating health impacts from pesticide poisonings—both the acute impacts mentioned in this study but also chronic exposures that farm workers and communities suffer.” Hélène Nicora, the director general of Parkinson’s Europe, said there was also “overwhelming evidence” to suggest that Parkinson’s was an environmentally driven disease, with  growing evidence  linking pesticide exposure to the development of Parkinson’s. Parkinson’s disease is a progressi
title: Study: Almost Half the World’s Farmers Are Poisoned by Pesticides Each Year
author: Pippa Neill

content: Sen. John Fetterman responded angrily this weekend to a recent Wall Street Journa l report, which quoted former staffers and the senator’s own alleged text messages to demonstrate his waning interest in performing basic job duties. The Pennsylvania Democrat, per the report, declined to meet with constituents, balked at attending a funeral for three slain police officers shot in York County, and asked why he had to keep meeting with representatives from the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. In an exclusive response to CNN, Fetterman called the reports about his attitude the work of “disgruntled staffers,” adding, “Per usual — lies, half-truths, innuendos, smears and anonymous.” An anonymous Twitter account claiming to represent former staffers was also created on Friday, promising that the WSJ story was, in the Twitter account’s words, “just the tip of the iceberg.” Fetterman, a first-term senator, has become, as one ex-staffer told Mother Jones last year, “Trump’s favorite Democrat .” He’s sided with Republicans on a myriad of issues, including voting against limiting Trump’s attack on Iran and taking a hard-line approach to immigration. He has rejected calls to shut down ICE and instead favors what he describes as “ commonsense reforms. ” (This despite the fact that his own wife, Gisele Barreto Fetterman, was herself previously undocumented. ) He’s also a strident backer of the Israeli government at a time when many Democrats are no longer defending Israel’s actions in Gaza and the West Bank; the WSJ report charged that he’s spent time courting conservative media and the pro-Israel advocates at the expense of many other constituencies. Much of the discussion about Fetterman has centered around how much his decision-making has been impacted by a stroke he suffered in 2022 while on the campaign trail. A May 2025 story in New York magazine reported on what staffers said was an alarming series of personality changes over time. His former chief of staff Adam Jentleson wrote in a 2024 memo quoted by the magazine that Fetterman was, in his words, “on a bad trajectory,” and outlined apparent impacts on his approach to work and policy: “Conspiratorial thinking; megalomania (for example, he claims to be the most knowledgeable source on Israel and Gaza around but his sources are just what he reads in the news — he declines most briefings and never reads memos); high highs and low lows; long, rambling, repetitive and self centered monologues; lying in ways that are painfully, awkwardly obvious to everyone in the room.” Fetterman has rejected reports from former staffers that he’s not fit to serve. In his response to CNN this weekend, he called the WSJ report “the third hit piece from disgruntled staffers” targeting him and claimed the cited text messages were “stripped of any context and circumstances.” He
title: John Fetterman Accuses “Disgruntled Staffers” of Spreading “Lies”
author: Anna Merlan

content: NA Each Labor Day since 2021, I have written posts explaining how breaking down barriers to labor mobility can help many millions of workers around the world. The main points everything last year's post are just as relevant today. So I am reprinting it with some updates and modifications, many of them related to the awful deterioration in immigration policy over the last year: Today is Labor Day. As usual, there is much discussion of what can be done to help workers. But few focus on the one type of reform that is likely to help more poor and disadvantaged workers than virtually anything else: increasing labor mobility. In the United States and around the world, far too many workers are trapped in places where it is difficult or impossible for them to ever escape poverty. They could vastly improve their lot if allowed to "vote with their feet" by moving to locations where there are better job opportunities. That would also be an enormous boon to the rest of society. Internationally, the biggest barriers condemning millions to lives of poverty and oppression are immigration restrictions. Economists estimate that eliminating legal barriers to migration throughout the world would roughly double world GDP - in other words, making the world twice as productive as it is now. A person who has the misfortune of being born in Cuba or Venezuela, Zimbabwe or Afghanistan, is likely condemned to lifelong poverty, no matter how talented or hardworking he or she may be. If they are allowed to move to a freer society with better economic institutions, they can almost immediately double or triple their income and productivity . And that doesn't consider the possibility of improving job skills, which is also likely to be more feasible in their new home than in their country of origin. The vast new wealth created by breaking down migration barriers would obviously benefit migrants themselves. But it also creates enormous advantages for receiving-country native s, as well. They benefit from cheaper and better products, increased innovation, and the establishment of new businesses (which immigrants create at higher rates than natives ). Immigrants also contribute disproportionately to scientific and medical innovation , including vaccines and other medical treatments that have already saved millions of lives around the world. The Trump Administration's massive assault on immigration of virtually every kind is predictably harming both migrants and native-born Americans, condemning hundreds of thousands of the former to a lifetime of poverty and oppression, and denying the latter the growth and innovation immigration facilitates. Most recently, thanks in part to a badly flawed Supreme Court decision , it has depriving hundreds of thousands of Haitians and others of legal status, thereby gravely harming both these migrants and the many US industries that depend on them. Similar, though somewhat less extreme, barriers to labor mobility also harm workers within the United
title: Help Workers by Breaking Down Barriers to Labor Mobility
author: Ilya Somin

content: The George W. Bush administration and its camp followers in the media sold the Iraq War with lies and spin. Before the war, hawkish pundits such as CNN host Fareed Zakaria and New York Times columnist Thomas L. Friedman promised that it would bring reform to the Arab world. Once the war started, Fox News host Brit Hume gloated that critics got it "completely wrong," and his colleague Tony Snow declared a "relatively bloodless victory"—two statements that aged very badly as the new Iraq collapsed into decades of war, with U.S. troops in the line of fire. So it went in Iran. Pro-war journalists and TV talking heads predicted that the Iranian government would collapse at the first push. Once the war started, they ignored signs that things were not going as planned. Unlike the Iraq War, the war in Iran has not turned into a drawn-out insurgency. The U.S. did not even topple the government, instead accepting a ceasefire after four weeks. But that ceasefire did not hold. At press time, the U.S. and Iran were fighting over the Strait of Hormuz, a key chokepoint for trade that had been fully open before the war. *** Before the U.S. attacked Iran on February 28, a chorus of media personalities, including several with direct lines to President Donald Trump, argued that a war with Iran would last only a few days . Washington Post columnist Marc Thiessen predicted that the Iranian government would quickly fall because "the Iranian people are the boots on the ground." Mark Dubowitz, CEO of the neoconservative Foundation for Defense of Democracies, told The Hugh Hewitt Show that Ali Khamenei, then Iran's supreme leader, would not fight back because "that's the end of his regime." Fox News host Mark Levin claimed Iran physically couldn't fight back. Reza Pahlavi, the crown prince of Iran overthrown in the 1979 revolution, was frequently featured on Fox News as a pro-war Iranian voice. Although he had some support among Iranians, the suburban dad formerly known as prince was making wild promises he couldn't keep. In a February 12 interview with the German magazine Der Spiegel , Pahlavi urged U.S. intervention, claiming he had recruited an army of 100,000 defectors. Not a single uprising against the Iranian government happened during the war. John Podhoretz, heir to the neoconservative magazine Commentary , at least admitted that his predictions fell flat. In the first hours of the war, he wrote that the U.S. military would leave "quick work for Iranians themselves to kick the mullahs to the curb." On a Commentary podcast four months later, he said "there is no person on Earth who is going to say that America didn't lose the war." Other pundits simply refused to acknowledge when things were not going their way. Week after week, Fox News commentator Jack Keane said the war would be over in two or three more weeks. Many of these pundits' arguments were simply an appeal to shut up and trust the leader. In mid-March, retired British Army officer Richard Kemp complain
title: The Iraq War Cheerleaders Were Wrong. They're Wrong About Iran Too.
author: Matthew Petti

content: There’s nothing to see here, folks. Don’t believe your lying eyes. The eldest son of the president of the United States and his investment firm, 1789 Capital, are raising money in a funding round for Polymarket, the gambling website that styles itself a “prediction market” and which Donald Trump Jr’s firm values at $21 billion. But it’s a nothingburger. Really. Except, if the relationship seems suspect on its face, that’s because it is. Trump Jr and his company stress that there’s a thick, heavy wall between his political connections — for instance, his father, the president — and his business activities. Never mind that, as the New York Times reports , the Trump family is invested in the “prediction market” business, and Trump Jr is an adviser for Polymarket and competitor Kalshi. Never mind that Trump Jr lobbied Republican state attorneys general to leave these companies alone as they sought regulatory capacity to rein in these gambling giants. So much for the wall between business and politics. The New Threat on the Block You can bet on just about anything on definitely-not-gambling sites like Polymarket and Kalshi. On an overcast Saturday morning, September 5, at 10:21 a.m. Eastern Standard Time, the “politics” tab on Polymarket’s site is offering odds on whether the Digital Asset Market Clarity (or CLARITY) Act will be signed into law (15 percent chance), the Federal Reserve rate decision in September (50 percent chance of a 25 basis points increase), and a Russia-Ukraine ceasefire by June 30, 2027 (57 percent). The CLARITY Act, introduced in Congress by a Republican lawmaker, and backed by Donald Trump, would regulate the cryptocurrency market. Last week, President Trump threatened to stop trading with some US partners unless the Fed cut interest rates. On the weekend, Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and US special envoy Steve Witkoff arrived in Moscow ahead of talks with Russia and Ukraine in an effort to end the war. A thick, heavy wall indeed. Scroll down any politics or economic market page on Polymarket, Kalshi, or any of the newfangled gambling platforms, and you’ll find no shortage of wagers that could be affected by the activities of someone in or close to the Trump family. The connection between the Trumps and the gambling markets is a prima facie conflict of interest — one that should matter in a sane, stable, democracy, but doesn’t seem to in the United States today. It’s a risk that won’t abate. In April, an American soldier was charged with using classified information to gamble on Polymarket, allegedly making more than $400,000 by misusing privileged information. The Anti-Corruption Data Collective has found evidence of more than 150 wallets on the platform that might be up to similar activities. In 2024, in the final hours of the Biden administration, someone made $300,000 betting on the outgoing president’s last-minute pardons. The profits were then sent to a crypto wallet. These stories are, predictably, a dime a dozen. La
title: Trump Family Prediction Market Conflicts Are a Good Bet
author: David Moscrop

content: A woman in a knit dress with flared sleeves works at an early model desktop computer in the 1970s. Hulton Archive/Getty Images During the early 20th century, women's employment was affected by war and advancements in tech. In the 1960s and 1970s, women expanded their horizons and career opportunities.  Vintage photos from the past 100 years show how their roles have changed. From factory floors to corner offices, women's roles in the workplace have undergone many reinventions over the past century. By the 1920s , decades of industrialization had drawn growing numbers of women into the workforce. Then, as men were sent off to war, more women entered the wartime effort in factories and other professions previously dominated by men. Women's equality movements  throughout the 1960s and 1970s gave working women more opportunities, and in recent years, the gap between men and women in the workforce has been closing, according to data released by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics. These vintage photos show how women's roles in the workforce have evolved over the last 100 years. In the wake of the Industrial Revolution, more women than ever began to leave the household and go out to work. Women postal workers at a sorting office, circa 1920. FPG/Hulton Archive/Getty Images Jobs commonly held by women included postal clerks, who sorted letters and packages. While it wasn't uncommon for women to work in post offices, very few women actually delivered mail. The US Postal Service reported that in 1920, only 5% of the nation's 943 village carriers were women.  As local postal delivery was gradually phased out in favor of larger city delivery, most of the remaining women village carriers either resigned or were transferred to clerk positions. Many women also began working in factories. Operating room of Ladies Rayon Undergarment Factory, 1920. George Rinhart/Corbis/Getty Images The US Department of Labor reported that in 1920, women made up about 20% of the labor force, an increase from previous generations. Many of them were involved in the production and manufacturing of clothing, food products, and tobacco products. Women of color, on the other hand, were largely employed in agriculture and domestic service work for much of the early 20th century. During World War I, women held occupations in domestic and personal service, clerical occupations, and factory work. Woman working in an office, USA, circa 1921. Universal History Archive/Universal Images Group/Getty Images Many women took typing courses to secure higher-paying jobs as secretaries or typists in clerical offices rather than working in factories. The Encyclopedia of Chicago reported that working conditions, wages, and hours in clerical work were seen as the best at the time. Clerical work attracted young, literate, mostly white women who would work as typists until they were married, only to be replaced by other young unmarried women when they left their jobs to raise their families.
title: Vintage photos show how the role of women in the workforce has evolved in the last 100 years
author: Erin McDowell (emcdowell@businessinsider.com)
