content: American socialists are convinced that they have a media-training problem. In the past year, members of the Democratic Socialists of America, the country’s largest leftist organization, have won electoral victories in places such as New York City and Michigan, drawing a spotlight that the group has struggled to handle. Last month, the DSA’s co-chairs, Megan Romer and Ashik Siddique, gave several high-profile interviews that even many of their most fervent supporters agree were disastrous. The two leaders struggled to give straight answers to simple questions, and they defended outlandish policies, such as abolishing prisons and police. They seemed to present socialists exactly the way their opponents caricature them: as extremist, unserious, and unprepared. In damage-control mode, many of DSA’s defenders on social media are repeating the phrase media training as though it were a mantra . If only the group’s leaders had been better prepared to deal with media outlets , the thinking goes, they would have avoided this train wreck . The DSA’s communications director, Priscilla Yeverino, recently told Axios , “Our leaders aren’t politicians. They’re working-class people and new to doing media.” The idea that the DSA’s troubles on prime-time television are a technical matter solvable by the right training is surely comforting, but it is also wrong. The group has a bigger problem: It is led by unpractical extremists whose views are a far cry from those that its electorally successful figures, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, espouse. [ Read: Why do rich kids love socialism? ] This disconnect is partly explained by a sharp division within the DSA. One wing engages in mass politics and includes AOC, Mamdani, and other socialists committed to democratic principles. The other wing is sectarian and extremist: It evinces little commitment to democracy and includes open admirers of Hamas, the Iranian regime, and historical dictators such as Mao Zedong. If the interviews with the DSA’s co-chairs were embarrassing, that’s a result not of a lackluster media performance but of the actual positions the group has embraced. A closer look at the interviews confirms this. Romer, who belongs to the sectarian wing, evidently did not know what the 2000 Camp David Summit was and could not say what “taxing the hell out of millionaires,” as she demanded, would look like in practice. When asked about authoritarianism in Cuba, she praised the country’s constitution and suggested that Americans should learn from it. Maybe media training could have taught Romer what happened at Camp David and what a tax policy might entail. It still wouldn’t have made the pro-authoritarian politics she shares with her faction of the DSA more palatable. In December, Romer’s Red Star caucus, a self-declared Marxist-Leninist faction of the DSA, posted quotes from a speech by Mao in “celebration” of the Chinese Communist leader’s 132nd birthday.
title: The DSA’s Problem Isn’t ‘Media Training’
author: Arash Azizi

content: Wendell Berry was not an easy man to reach. When I wanted to interview him for this magazine in the spring of 2015, his publicist warned me that a press request would take some doing. Berry didn’t have a cellphone. He didn’t use email. He didn’t even have a computer. He wrote most of his drafts by hand during the day, without electric light. And he definitely didn’t make himself available to any old reporter who wanted to talk. I knew this already, of course. Berry, who died on Monday at the age of 92, lived a life defined by acts of radical abstention. He said no emphatically and often; principled refusal was a central theme of his writing and the lore that surrounded him. The publicist spent the better part of a week trying to reach Berry on my behalf. This involved multiple phone calls to his farmhouse, in Henry County, Kentucky, where Berry and his wife, Tanya, had lived since the mid-1960s. Wendell spent most of his time outdoors, the publicist explained, so he often simply wasn’t around to hear the landline ring. After a while, though, she told me that she and Berry had managed to connect, and that he would consider my request. He asked that I write him a letter about the article I had in mind, which I emailed to the publicist so she could print it out and send it to him by post. [ From the February 1991 issue: Out of your car, off your horse ] A few weeks later, I received a voicemail from a number I didn’t recognize. “Hello, Mr. Fassler,” said a voice that was deep and hoarse with age. “This is Wendell Berry.” A giant of Luddism was speaking out of my iPhone. He asked me to call him back. When we spoke, he told me in a warm, genial way that I was out of luck. “I’m just so covered up with work,” he said, “and I can’t tell if it’s because I’m just busy or because I’m old.” But he’d thought a bit about my letter. I’d asked him to take part in “ By Heart ,” a series in which authors discussed the passages from literature that had most shaped their writing and outlook. He said that his forthcoming book, Our Only World , contained a section that the magazine might adapt in some way. It hinged on some verses from Jesus’s Sermon on the Mount, as described in the Gospel of Matthew: “Take no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” He asked me to read that section of his book, and to call him back once I had so that we could talk. So I did. And I’ve been thinking about its message ever since. I was surprised, at first, that Berry felt so drawn to this specific moment from the Bible. Jesus’s instruction to not worry about the future seemed at odds with much of what Berry had written. Many of the social and environmental problems that Berry railed against were really problems of short-term thinking, including the pursuit of quick profit, the extractive poisoning of the land, and the love of cheap thrills over deeper, more hard-won pleasures. “Think not of tomorro
title: Why Wendell Berry Didn’t Worry About the Future
author: Joe Fassler

content: Students returning to campus this semester are arriving with a great deal of anxiety about AI and what it will mean for their lives after college. They are right to be worried. New research from Stanford shows that, even though the much-hyped AI job apocalypse has yet to materialize, the technology has already caused a nearly 20 percent drop in employment for young workers in AI-exposed occupations, such as computer programming and customer-service work. Anxiety over the looming threat of AI may seem novel, but as a cognitive scientist who has long studied how fear affects learning and performance, I am all too familiar with this kind of unease. This is how I know it is also curable. Several years ago, my former graduate student Ian Lyons and I invited people who were anxious about math to have their brains scanned while they took a math test. We were surprised to find that it wasn’t the test itself that sent people’s brains into a panic. Rather, the neural signals associated with threat detection and pain were most acute when people were merely anticipating the test. [ John Paul Rollert: A society of cheats ] We are all now living through AI’s waiting-for-the-math-test phase. AI is transforming classrooms, workplaces, and hiring needs—and experts say more turbulence is coming. Teachers and students are struggling to parse the difference between deploying AI effectively and exploiting the technology to cheat. But rather than tackling this disruptive change and the resulting anxiety head-on, many educators are trying to make AI simply go away. The University of Chicago’s social-science faculty have prohibited most technology and banned the use of AI tools from their core classes. Although law firms are beginning to embrace the benefits of generative AI, the technology apparently makes many law schools squeamish. In May, the UC Berkeley School of Law announced that students are prohibited from using AI in “conceptualizing, outlining, drafting, revising, translating, or editing any work submitted for credit.” The University of Chicago Law School has decided to ban all screens from first-year classrooms entirely. In an atmosphere of uncertainty—and given prevailing concerns about students using AI to cheat—such bans would seem to make some sense. But draconian mandates and screenless classes can’t be the only ways that colleges deal with AI. If universities hope to remain relevant in a world shaped by artificial intelligence, they should strive to guide students to understand and use these tools productively. In my research of math anxiety, we found that the best cure was practicing math. This points to a way forward. When we supply students with the space to thoughtfully explore and engage with these tools, we can help ensure that they graduate into an AI-enabled workforce with more confidence and competence than fear, and with an appreciation for how to use AI tools ethically. But if higher education opts for prohibition over practice, we will squa
title: Why I Want More AI at Dartmouth
author: Sian Leah Beilock

content: America’s older adults are a growing share of the population, but the systems meant to support them haven’t kept up. Older adults and their families struggle to access essential services and barriers hit hardest for select populations, such as people with disabilities, individuals with low incomes, veterans, and rural communities. Policymakers have taken steps to strengthen the nation’s aging system, which provides services to millions of older adults, people with disabilities, and family caregivers. However, progress has been slow, and the existing challenges are worsening as the baby boomer generation ages. Continued inaction will leave Americans without the supports they need to age with dignity, harming older adults and their families while driving up avoidable federal and state costs. The Older Americans Act is a core federal law addressing aging. Congress last reauthorized the law in 2020, with funding authorized through 2024. Congress has since funded the programs at the 2024 levels through continuing resolutions. Most recently, the Senate unanimously passed its version of an extension, the Older Americans Act Reauthorization Act of 2025 . The House has not yet considered the reauthorizing legislation. Through our Aging of America Initiative: Forging a National Consensus for 2029 , the Bipartisan Policy Center is identifying policy recommendations that lower everyday costs and enhance support for older adults and caregivers, strengthen retirement security, and ensure the long-term sustainability of key programs. As policymakers work to close these persistent gaps, understanding the shifting policy landscape is essential to building durable, bipartisan solutions. This article highlights select emerging policy changes BPC is monitoring across three persisting challenges: 1) long-term care, 2) housing, and 3) nutrition . Join BPC’s webinar on July 28 from 1 to 2 p.m. ET to hear from leading experts on these challenges, including the evolving policy landscape and evidence-based solutions to help Americans age with dignity. 1. How is the Long-Term Care System Not Meeting the Needs of Older Adults, People with Disabilities, and Their Families? With the population over 85 projected to almost double from 7 million to nearly 14 million from 2025 to 2040, demand for long-term care will keep rising. When people cannot access the long-term care they need, their health and independence suffer and the strain on family caregivers grows. Medicare generally does not cover long-term care, and complex market challenges have put private insurance out of reach for many.  Millions are forced to spend down their personal net worth to become eligible for Medicaid, which covers long-term care. Many also choose to rely on unpaid family caregivers, a substantial number of whom risk their own financial security by reducing their work hours or leaving the workforce entirely. Access to these services is further limited due to a persistent shortag
title: How Policy Changes Are Reshaping Aging in America
author: Allison Buffett, Daisy Kim, Kamryn Perry

content: The research takeaways section of the AI and Workforce Navigator is designed to address the most pressing questions policymakers have with the latest research. New research and news about AI’s impacts on jobs and workers is published daily and it can be difficult to know what is important. These questions are updated quarterly to reflect timely concerns and keep up with the rapid pace of change. As new questions arise, previous questions will be archived in an article so that research insights will remain accessible. You can read more about AI’s impact on the additional resources page of the Navigator How widespread is AI use in the workforce and where is it most prevalent? There are many types of AI including generative, predictive, agentic, and physical. Generative AI (GenAI) has seen particularly broad usage, with roughly 40% of workers using it in their jobs. Workers most commonly use GenAI for tasks requiring reasoning, communication, or problem-solving—including writing, editing, research, and coding. AI use is generally highest in knowledge-based sectors like information technology (42%) and professional and technical services (37%), and lowest in sectors requiring physical work like agriculture (4%) and accommodation and food services (8%). Is AI causing jobs to disappear entirely? Right now, there is no evidence of widespread job elimination; instead, AI tends to affect specific tasks within jobs, and its early effects are likely to show up in hiring patterns and skills demand rather than widespread worker displacement or elimination of entire roles. High exposure to AI means a job has tasks that overlap with AI capabilities, but that doesn’t automatically translate into job losses. AI may augment workers in those tasks rather than replace them, making them more productive rather than redundant. Even where AI can automate tasks, it rarely automates entire jobs—regulatory barriers, organizational context, and the limits of what AI can do all constrain how far automation goes. However, if a significant proportion of tasks in a job are automated, that could lead to worker displacement. Though the evidence is still emerging and broader economic factors may be playing a role, there are early signs of a hiring slowdown for entry-level office-based roles, which are particularly exposed to AI. Of the 37 million U.S. workers in the most AI-exposed occupations, around six million face both high exposure and limited capacity to adapt to other roles or industries. They are concentrated in clerical and administrative roles, overwhelmingly female, and often located in mid-sized cities with fewer local job alternatives. While we haven’t seen entire roles disappear yet, caution is warranted: policymakers should not interpret the absence of early large-scale job loss as a permanent trend. Additionally, policymakers should be cautious about correlating AI exposure with likelihood of displacement. The more useful question is how AI is being adopted i
title: Q1 AI Insights for Policy Makers: April 2026
author: Michelle Kumar, Rachel Schick, Jack Malde
